bull_thesis:
Olema is one molecule and one experiment, and the experiment lands within weeks. Palazestrant is a once-daily pill for the most common form of advanced breast cancer, the kind that grows in response to oestrogen. It is designed to shut the oestrogen receptor down completely, blocking both of the receptor's activation switches and degrading the receptor itself, where the pills already approved in this class reliably block only one. The pivotal study, OPERA-01, enrolled about 510 patients whose disease had already progressed on hormone therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor, and it tests palazestrant on its own against whatever single hormone drug the treating physician would otherwise choose.

Three things carry the bullish case. First, the trial is built to win broadly. Results are reported separately in patients whose tumours carry an ESR1 mutation, a genetic change that develops under hormone therapy in roughly four of ten patients, and separately in patients who do not carry it. Olema could have registered a mutation-only study and secured a likely approval in a small niche; it deliberately took on the harder population, which is where the whole commercial prize sits. Second, the comparator is weak: these are patients on their second or third line of treatment, measured against a single hormone drug, which historically buys them only a couple of months before the disease grows again. Third, the balance sheet removes the usual way biotech investors lose money before a readout. Olema held $505.3 million of cash and marketable securities against under $1 million of debt on 31 March 2026, with no covenants and no maturity wall, and it raised $213.6 million in the fourth quarter of 2025 when the shares were near their $36.26 high. The event is fully paid for. There is no financing contingency and no need to come to market at $11 before the data.

The timing is live and has not slipped. Management guided to top-line results in the fall of 2026 when it reported first-quarter figures on 12 May 2026 and reaffirmed that window publicly at the Goldman Sachs healthcare conference on 9 June 2026. The trial registry lists an estimated primary completion date of 30 June 2026, which has now passed. There has been no company announcement of any kind since 2 June 2026, so the event has neither fired nor been withdrawn.

There is also a second leg that the market is close to valuing at nothing. OP-3136, a KAT6 inhibitor, showed no dose-limiting toxicities and no discontinuations for drug-related side effects in initial Phase 1 data presented on 21 May 2026, and Bayer signed a clinical collaboration on 26 May 2026 to test it alongside its prostate-cancer drug NUBEQA in about 36 patients. A large partner putting its own approved drug and its own patients behind an unproven molecule is a real, if modest, external vote.

For this to work, one condition must hold above all others: palazestrant has to show a clear delay in disease progression in patients WITHOUT an ESR1 mutation, not only in those who carry one. That is the outcome no drug in this class has yet achieved, and it is the difference between a company worth roughly $25 a share and one worth roughly $11.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require the drug to fail. It only requires the drug to succeed in the way every predecessor in its class has succeeded.

The prior pivotal studies of oral oestrogen-receptor degraders in this same second-line setting delivered convincing benefit in patients carrying an ESR1 mutation and failed to demonstrate the same in the broader mutation-negative population. That is why the one approved drug in the class carries a mutation-restricted label. If OPERA-01 repeats that pattern, Olema becomes the third or fourth entrant into a niche that is already served, arriving after the incumbents, and the equity is worth roughly what it trades for today. The single most likely outcome is therefore not a loss and not a win. It is par.

The second leg of the bear case is arithmetic, and it is the finding that changes this file. The share count is about 18% larger than every headline screen shows. The cover page of the 31 March 2026 quarterly filing reports 87,347,471 common shares outstanding, and both the market-data feed and the public screening sites use that figure, which is why they print a market value of $1.00 billion and an enterprise value of about $499 million. But the same filing computes its loss per share on a weighted average of 102,800,098 shares, and the company's own arithmetic confirms it: a net loss of $53.089 million divided by the reported loss per share of $0.52 gives 102.1 million. The roughly 15.5 million share gap is the signature of pre-funded warrants, which are shares already paid for at a nominal exercise price and are economically identical to stock. On the true count, the market value at $11.45 is $1.18 billion, the enterprise value is $673 million rather than $499 million, and net cash is $4.91 a share rather than $5.77. Every per-share number in the bull case is about 18% smaller than it appears.

Third, the burn is accelerating and the company is diluting into the decline. Research spending was $49.2 million in the first quarter of 2026 against $30.6 million a year earlier, a rise of about 61%, and operating cash burn was $46.0 million in the quarter. The cash-flow statement also shows $50.1 million of stock issued in the first quarter of 2026, a period in which the shares roughly halved. Management is also running a roughly 1,000-patient first-line study before knowing whether the second-line trial works, which adds burn now and adds shares later if the answer is bad.

Fourth, the date is soft. This is a company-guided season, not a regulatory decision date. No third party is obliged to act. The trial reports when enough disease-progression events accumulate, a statistical trigger management does not fully control, so a slip into December is possible without anyone having misled anybody. The registry record itself is stale: it was last updated on 13 March 2026, its status was last verified in August 2025, and it still reads recruiting for a trial that should have finished enrolling long ago.

What would confirm the bear case: a second-quarter report on 10 August 2026 that softens the fall window or shows continued market-price stock issuance; or a top-line release that reports a clear result in mutation-positive patients and a miss or a marginal result in everyone else.
sop_bull:
The event-win value, meaning a clear delay in disease progression in BOTH the ESR1-mutation-positive and the mutation-negative populations: about $24 a share.

Derivation, on the corrected economic share count of about 102.8 million units rather than the 87.3 million the screens use. A palazestrant that clears both populations is a genuine oral standard of care in second-line-and-beyond ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, with a credible path into first line through the roughly 1,000-patient study already running. A de-risked pivotal winner with a broad label in an indication of this size supports a risk-adjusted enterprise value of roughly $2.0 to $2.2 billion, whether the company stays independent or is acquired, which is the usual outcome for a single-asset company holding clean pivotal data in a large solid-tumour market. Add the roughly $390 million of cash expected to remain at the readout and the equity is worth about $2.4 to $2.6 billion, or $24 to $25 a share.

Overlays: net cash of $504.4 million at 31 March 2026 ($505.347 million of cash and marketable securities less $0.956 million of debt) is the only balance-sheet item of consequence. There are no pending distributions, no announced asset sales and no deal terms. OP-3136 is left uncredited in this case because a broad palazestrant win subsumes it in the multiple.

sop_bear:
The verified downside floor, meaning neither population reaches statistical significance: about $3.90 a share.

Derivation, and it is almost entirely cash rather than judgement. Olema held $505.3 million of cash and marketable securities against $0.956 million of debt on 31 March 2026, giving net cash of $504.4 million. Operating cash burn was $46.0 million in the first quarter of 2026 and research spending is rising sharply, so roughly $50 million a quarter is the right run rate. Seven months to a late-October readout consumes about $117 million, leaving approximately $390 million. On the corrected economic count of about 102.8 million units that is $3.79 a share of net cash.

Two adjustments in opposite directions, and they roughly cancel. Upward: OP-3136 retains real residual value after a palazestrant failure, having shown no dose-limiting toxicities and no discontinuations for drug-related side effects in Phase 1 data on 21 May 2026, with Bayer committing its own approved drug to a combination study on 26 May 2026 — call it $60 to $100 million. Downward: a company whose lead asset has just failed a pivotal trial routinely trades at 70 to 90 cents on the dollar of its cash for months afterwards, because the market assumes the cash will be spent rather than returned.

Net floor: $3.90 a share, with a realistic bad-tape band of $3.25 to $4.50.

This is materially below both the $6.50 floor carried on our catalyst board and the $4.25 used in the previous review, and the entire difference is the share count. The floor is genuinely real — it is cash in the bank, with no debt, no covenants and no going-concern language — but it sits 66% below the current price. It is a backstop, not a cushion.
sop_breakdown:
Probability-weighted across three discrete outcomes, because the honest distribution here has two humps rather than a smooth range. All per-share figures use the corrected economic share count of about 102.8 million units, not the 87.3 million common shares the screens use.

Broad win, meaning a clear delay in disease progression in both the mutation-positive and the mutation-negative populations: 22% probability, $24.00 a share. This is the outcome the trial was deliberately designed to chase and the only one that justifies the sell-side's models.

Narrow win, meaning a clear result in mutation-positive patients only: 45% probability, $11.00 a share. This is the single most likely outcome and it is worth roughly today's price, because it makes Olema the third or fourth entrant into a niche the incumbents already serve. It is also the outcome the prior pivotal trials in this class produced, which is why the one approved drug in the class carries a mutation-restricted label. Enterprise value of roughly $650 to $750 million plus about $390 million of cash gives $10 to $11 a share.

Clean failure, meaning neither analysis succeeds: 33% probability, $3.90 a share, backed by roughly $390 million of unencumbered cash at the readout plus partial credit for OP-3136, offset by the discount to cash a failed lead normally carries.

Weighted: 0.22 times $24.00, plus 0.45 times $11.00, plus 0.33 times $3.90, equals $11.52, rounded to $11.50.

Cross-check on the enterprise value: at $11.45 a share the true economic market value is $1.18 billion and the enterprise value is $673 million, so about 43% of the share price is cash in the bank. The market is paying $673 million for a pivotal-stage asset worth roughly $2.1 billion if it wins broadly and about $700 million if it wins narrowly. Given the base rate in this drug class, that is a coherent price for the odds, not a mispricing. Note that screens showing a $499 million enterprise value are understating it by about a third because they use the cover-page share count.
risk_reward:
Upside to the $24.00 event-win target is plus 110% from $11.45. Downside to the verified $3.90 floor is minus 66%. That is about 1.7 to 1 on the two tails, which sounds attractive until it is weighted. Measured against the probability-weighted fair value of $11.50, the edge from today's price is about plus 0.4% — effectively zero.

That is the whole finding. The reason is not that the catalyst fired or that the story broke; neither happened. It is that the shares fell 54% this year, and the economic share count is about 18% larger than the headline screens show. Put those together and the price today sits at roughly the value of the MOST LIKELY outcome — a win confined to mutation-positive patients — rather than at a discount to it. An investor buying here pays par for the modal case in order to hold a roughly one-in-five ticket on a double, against a one-in-three chance of losing about two-thirds. That is a fair coin, not an edge.

The price that restores a genuine margin — a 25% to 30% discount to the weighted value, which is the standard this book applies — is roughly $8.00 to $8.60.

positioning_washout:
The forced selling is real, it has been running for six months, and — importantly for the timing call — it does not look finished.

The shape of it: the shares are down 54% this year, 56% over six months, 20% over three months and 10% over the past month, against a 200-day average of $17.45 and a 52-week high of $36.26 set during the late-2025 enthusiasm. Start with what is verified. The second is a base rate. The prior pivotal trials of oral oestrogen-receptor degraders in this same second-line setting won in ESR1-mutation-positive patients and did not convincingly win beyond them, which is why the one approved drug in the class carries a mutation-restricted label. That is the verdict in one line: after a 54% decline this year, the market is now paying almost exactly the value of the single most likely outcome. An investor buying at $11.45 pays par for the modal case in order to hold a one-in-five ticket on a double, against a one-in-three chance of losing two-thirds. It is a fair coin. This funnel exists to find defined-risk asymmetry, and the discipline is to give a live dated catalyst the high conviction it earns — but the same discipline requires naming it when the asymmetry is not there, and here it is not. The previous review's higher score rested on a $14.50 fair value that the share-count correction removes.

So: wait, and name the level. Nothing about the catalyst needs to improve for this to become interesting; only the price does. The entry that restores the 25% to 30% margin this book requires is roughly $8.00 to $8.60. The tape argues that level is reachable — the shares have fallen about 10% a month on no news, the five-day move is a flat 0.4%, and there is no sign of a capitulation flush having happened yet. Two developments would change the call before then: a second-quarter report on 10 August 2026 that reaffirms the fall window while showing the market-price stock issuance has stopped would firm up both the date and the floor; a report that softens the window, or shows continued issuance, would take this to a pass.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

on the dollar of cash for months. Those two effects roughly cancel. A realistic bad-tape band is
**$3.25 to $4.50**.

The floor is *real* — it is cash in the bank, not a promise — but it sits **66% below the current
price**. That is a backstop, not a cushion.

## 4. MANAGEMENT CREDIBILITY ON THE EVENT

🟢 **They funded the event at the right price.** Olema raised $213.6 million in the fourth quarter of
2025, when the stock was near its high of $36.26. The event is fully paid for; there is no financing
contingency and no need to come to market at $11 before the data. This is the single best thing on
the record and it removes the usual way investors lose money in the months before a readout.

🟢 **Guidance has never been softened.** The fall-2026 window was stated on 12 May 2026 and
reaffirmed publicly on 9 June 2026. No hedging language has appeared.

🟢 **They chose the harder trial.** Olema could have registered a study restricted to patients whose
tumours carry an ESR1 mutation — a genetic change that develops under hormone therapy in roughly
four in ten patients — and secured a likely approval in a defined niche. It deliberately powered the
trial to report separately in mutation-positive and mutation-negative patients, which is where the
commercial prize actually sits.

🔴 **They kept selling stock into the decline.** The cash-flow statement shows $50.1 million of stock
issued in the first quarter of 2026, a period in which the shares roughly halved. That is a
market-price programme running while the equity was already de-rating, and it is why the share count
is where it is.

🔴 **Spending ahead of the answer.** Launching a 1,000-patient first-line study before the pivotal
second-line trial reports adds burn and adds shares if the answer is bad.

🔴 **The registry has not been maintained.** Not a fraud signal, but the record of a company that
either is not watching that page or does not want to timestamp enrolment completion.

## 5. THE PRESSURE POINT NOBODY IS ADDRESSING

The sell-side has gone quiet at exactly the moment its numbers stopped making sense. Seven firms
carry Buy or Overweight ratings — Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan, Citigroup, Guggenheim, Oppenheimer, HC
Wainwright — and the average published target over the past year is **$37.86**, with the most recent
at $35. The last rating action of any kind was 13 May 2026. There have been **no price-target updates
in the last month** while the stock fell 10%, and none at all while it fell 54% this year.

Nobody wants to be the analyst who cuts a target seven weeks before a binary readout. The published
targets are therefore stale anchors, not live estimates, and the roughly three-times gap between the
$35 consensus and the $11.45 price is not an opportunity signal — it is evidence that the models have
not been marked.

## 6. THE BASE RATE THE BULL CASE HAS TO BEAT

This class of drug has a track record, and it is not encouraging for the broad win. The prior
pivotal studies of oral oestrogen-receptor degraders in this same second-line setting delivered
convincing benefit in ESR1-mutation-positive patients and failed to demonstrate the same in the
broader mutation-negative population — which is why the one approved drug in the class, elacestrant,
carries a mutation-restricted label. Palazestrant's mechanism is genuinely differentiated and the
comparator in OPERA-01 (a single physician's-choice hormone drug, in patients on their second or
third line) is weak. But the honest prior for a clean win in *both* populations is well under half.

## 7. RED FLAGS CHECKED AND CLEARED

- Going concern: **none**. Roughly two years of runway at the current burn.
- Debt / covenants / maturity wall: **none**. Total debt is under $1 million.
- Financing contingency on the catalyst: **none**. Fully funded through the readout.
- Regulatory second request, deal break, contingent-value-right games: **not applicable** — this is a
  data readout, not a transaction.
- Dilution: **live and ongoing** via the at-the-market programme. This is the one real red flag, and
  it is already reflected in the corrected share count above.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: **stable**. The trial is on track, guidance has been reaffirmed twice, and the balance
sheet fully funds the answer.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing:** the spread has closed, and not for the
reason it usually does. The catalyst has not fired and the story has not broken. What happened is
that the stock fell 54% this year, and the share count is 18% larger than the screens show. Put
those together and the price today sits at roughly the value of the *most likely* outcome — a win
confined to mutation-positive patients — rather than at a discount to it. An investor buying here is
paying par for the modal case in order to hold a roughly one-in-five ticket on a double, against a
one-in-three chance of losing about two-thirds. That is a fair coin, not an edge.

The name deserves a standing bid, not a position at this price. Nothing about the catalyst needs to
improve for this to become interesting; only the price does.

Economic moat: none, and none is expected — this is a single-asset clinical company. No structural
force threatens a terminal value that does not yet exist.
